[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Non-linear Transformations: PowerTransformer and QuantileTransformer in Scikit-learn"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Many machine learning algorithms assume that input features are normally distributed (Gaussian). When faced with heavily skewed data, models like linear regression, support vector machines, and neural networks can suffer in performance. Scikit-learn provides two powerful preprocessing utilities for non-linear transformations: PowerTransformer and QuantileTransformer. This tutorial explores how to use both transformers to map arbitrary data distributions to a Gaussian distribution."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Power Transformations"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Power transformations are a family of parametric, monotonic transformations that aim to map data from any distribution to as close to a normal distribution as possible. This helps to stabilize variance and minimize skewness. Scikit-learn implements two primary methods within the PowerTransformer class:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Box-Cox: Supports only strictly positive data values."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Yeo-Johnson: Supports both positive and zero/negative data values."},{"order":7,"type":"heading","text":"Implementing PowerTransformer"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Let us look at how to apply the Yeo-Johnson power transformation to a synthetic skewed dataset using Python and Scikit-learn."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Generate skewed data (exponential distribution)
rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.exponential(scale=2.0, size=(1000, 1))

# Initialize PowerTransformer
pt = PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson')
X_transformed = pt.fit_transform(X)

print('Original mean:', np.mean(X), 'variance:', np.var(X))
print('Transformed mean:', np.mean(X_transformed), 'variance:', np.var(X_transformed))"},{"order":10,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Quantile Transformers"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike PowerTransformer, which relies on parametric maximum likelihood estimation, the QuantileTransformer applies a non-linear transformation to map the data to a uniform or a normal distribution based on the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the features. This has the effect of spreading out the most frequent values and reducing the impact of outliers."},{"order":12,"type":"heading","text":"Implementing QuantileTransformer"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"The following code snippet demonstrates how to map features to a normal distribution using the QuantileTransformer class."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import QuantileTransformer

# Generate heavy-tailed data with outliers
X_outliers = np.concatenate([rng.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=(900, 1)), rng.uniform(loc=10, scale=20, size=(100, 1))])

# Initialize QuantileTransformer to output a normal distribution
qt = QuantileTransformer(output_distribution='normal', random_state=42)
X_qt_transformed = qt.fit_transform(X_outliers)

print('Quantile transformed shape:', X_qt_transformed.shape)"},{"order":15,"type":"heading","text":"Comparing PowerTransformer and QuantileTransformer"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PowerTransformer is parametric and robust for smaller datasets, but it strictly requires tuning parameters and assumes a monotonic mapping to normality."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"QuantileTransformer is non-parametric, highly effective at handling extreme outliers by smoothing them out, but it can heavily distort linear correlations between features."},{"order":18,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Choosing between PowerTransformer and QuantileTransformer depends heavily on your specific machine learning pipeline and data characteristics. Always evaluate downstream model performance using cross-validation to decide which non-linear transformation yields the best generalization."}]
